title: Regular Queue (FIFO)
description: FIFO enqueue and dequeue, front and rear pointers, false overflow, and pointer reset on the bounded linear array queue used by regular-queue.html.

questions.prompt: You enqueue 10, then 20, then 30 into an empty regular queue, and then call dequeue(). Which value is removed?
choices: Nothing: dequeue requires choosing which element to remove
questions.explanation: A regular queue follows First-In, First-Out (FIFO), so dequeue always removes the oldest element at the front, which is 10. Picking 30 is the most tempting mistake if you confuse a queue with a LIFO stack, where the newest value leaves first.
questions.page: On regular-queue.html: set queue size 5, enqueue 10, 20, and 30, then type 10 and press Dequeue (Front).

questions.prompt: In LinearQueue on regular-queue.html, a newly allocated empty queue starts with front = 0 and rear = -1.
questions.explanation: LinearQueue initializes front to 0 and rear to -1 so the first enqueue increments rear to 0 and writes Q[0], giving front = rear = 0 for a single element. Answering False is tempting if you expect both pointers to start at 0 or both at -1 (as in CircularQueue), but starting rear at 0 would make an empty queue indistinguishable from a one-element queue.
questions.page: On regular-queue.html: enter 5 in Max size (1-100), press Set Queue Size, and read the state banner.

questions.prompt: Starting from an empty linear queue with capacity 5: enqueue 4, enqueue 9, dequeue, enqueue 2. List the remaining elements from front to rear.
questions.hint: Track both front and rear after each operation; dequeue removes from the front and enqueue appends at the rear.
questions.explanation: Enqueue 4 and 9 gives [4, 9] with 4 at the front. Dequeue removes 4 (FIFO), leaving [9]. Enqueue 2 appends 2 at the rear, giving [9, 2]. Answering "4, 2" removes the newest value 9 instead of the oldest value 4, which is stack behavior rather than queue behavior.
questions.page: On regular-queue.html: set queue size 5, enqueue 4 and 9, dequeue 4, then enqueue 2.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of enqueue(x) on this fixed-capacity linear array queue?
questions.explanation: enqueue(x) checks rear == capacity - 1, increments rear by 1, writes Q[rear] = x, and increments count—a fixed number of steps no matter how many items are queued. O(n) is tempting if you think elements must shift when inserting, but only the rear index advances.

questions.prompt: On regular-queue.html, the queue holds [12, 25] with 12 at the front and 25 at the rear. You type 25 into the value box and click Dequeue (Front). What happens?
choices: Nothing is removed: the page reminds you that only the front (12) can be dequeued
25 is removed from the rear of the queue
12 is dequeued anyway and 25 is ignored
questions.answer: Nothing is removed: the page reminds you that only the front (12) can be dequeued
questions.explanation: To reinforce FIFO, regular-queue.html asks you to confirm the front value before dequeuing; typing 25 shows "Only the front can leave a queue. The front is 12. Type 12 to dequeue it." and leaves the queue unchanged. Removing 25 is tempting if you think of a stack or double-ended queue, not a FIFO queue.
questions.page: On regular-queue.html: set queue size 4, enqueue 12 and 25, type 25, and press Dequeue (Front).

questions.prompt: A linear queue has capacity 4 (indices 0 to 3). You enqueue 10, 20, 30, then dequeue once, then enqueue 40. What is the rear index afterwards?
questions.hint: Does dequeue move rear backward, or does it only advance front?
questions.explanation: Enqueuing 10, 20, and 30 advances rear to 0, 1, and 2. Dequeue moves front from 0 to 1 and leaves rear at 2. Enqueuing 40 increments rear to 3. Answering 2 assumes dequeue shifted elements left or decremented rear, which a linear array queue never does.
questions.page: On regular-queue.html: set queue size 4, enqueue 10, 20, 30, dequeue 10, enqueue 40, and check rear.

questions.prompt: In a LinearQueue of capacity 4, you enqueue 1, 2, 3, 4 and then dequeue 1. Calling isFull() now returns true.
questions.explanation: isFull() checks count == capacity. After four enqueues and one dequeue, count is 3 while capacity is 4, so isFull() returns false even though rear == 3 blocks further enqueues (false overflow). Answering True is the classic trap of confusing "rear is at the end" with "every slot holds a value."
questions.page: On regular-queue.html: set queue size 4, enqueue 1, 2, 3, 4, dequeue 1, then press isFull?.

questions.prompt: Which of these operations run in O(1) time on LinearQueue? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: enqueue, dequeue, peek, and peekRear each inspect or update at most one array slot (Q[front] or Q[rear]) and integer indices, so they are O(1). clear() calls slots.fill(null) across all capacity slots, taking O(capacity) time (linear in the allocated size, not O(1))—a tempting wrong pick if you assume clearing only resets front and rear.

questions.prompt: A linear queue has capacity 4. You enqueue 5, 6, 7, 8, then dequeue twice (removing 5 and 6), then try to enqueue 9. How many wasted (freed and unusable) slots sit before front afterwards?
questions.hint: Check whether enqueue 9 succeeds when rear is already at index 3, and count the empty slots before front.
questions.explanation: After enqueuing 5, 6, 7, and 8, rear is 3 (the last index). Two dequeues free indices 0 and 1 and advance front to 2, leaving 2 wasted slots before front. Enqueuing 9 fails with false overflow and changes nothing, so wastedSlots stays 2. Answering 1 assumes 9 reused index 0, which only happens in a circular queue.
questions.page: On regular-queue.html: set queue size 4, enqueue 5, 6, 7, 8, dequeue 5 and 6, then try to enqueue 9.

questions.prompt: On regular-queue.html, which capacity value is rejected by Set Queue Size?
questions.explanation: LinearQueue accepts whole-number capacities from 1 through 100 (LinearQueue.MAX_CAPACITY = 100), so 101 is rejected. Choosing 1 is the most tempting mistake because CircularQueue requires a minimum capacity of 2, whereas LinearQueue permits a 1-slot queue.
questions.page: On regular-queue.html: type 101 into Max size (1-100) and press Set Queue Size.

questions.prompt: A linear queue has capacity 3 (indices 0 to 2). You enqueue 7, enqueue 8, dequeue, dequeue, and then enqueue 9. What is the rear index after enqueuing 9?
questions.hint: What does LinearQueue.dequeue() do to front and rear when count drops to 0?
questions.explanation: After enqueuing 7 and 8, front = 0 and rear = 1. The first dequeue removes 7 (front = 1, count = 1); the second removes 8 and drops count to 0, which resets front = 0 and rear = -1. Enqueuing 9 then moves rear from -1 to 0. Answering 2 is the tempting mistake if you forget the empty-queue pointer reset.
questions.page: On regular-queue.html: set queue size 3, enqueue 7 and 8, dequeue 7 and 8, then enqueue 9.

questions.prompt: Once a linear queue enters false overflow (rear == capacity - 1 while count < capacity), the only way on regular-queue.html to enqueue again without clicking Clear All or Reset Queue is to dequeue every remaining element until the queue becomes empty.
questions.explanation: While count > 0, dequeue() only increments front and leaves rear stuck at capacity - 1, so enqueue() keeps failing with false overflow. Only when the last element leaves (count == 0) does LinearQueue reset front = 0 and rear = -1, unblocking enqueue. Answering False is tempting if you think freeing one more slot allows enqueue to succeed.
questions.page: On regular-queue.html: fill a size-3 queue, dequeue one item, see enqueue fail, then dequeue the remaining two items and enqueue again.

questions.prompt: Suppose you tried to eliminate false overflow in a linear array queue of n elements by shifting every remaining element one slot left inside dequeue(). What would the worst-case time complexity of dequeue() become?
questions.explanation: Moving all n - 1 remaining elements one index left during dequeue takes time proportional to n, degrading dequeue() from O(1) to O(n). O(1) is tempting because pointer-only dequeue is O(1), and avoiding this O(n) shift is the exact reason circular queues wrap indices with modulo instead.

questions.prompt: A LinearQueue of capacity 3 runs: enqueue 1, enqueue 2, enqueue 3, dequeue, enqueue 4. Which statements are TRUE right after the enqueue(4) call? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: After dequeuing 1, slots are [null, 2, 3] with front = 1, rear = 2, and count = 2. enqueue(4) fails with false overflow and mutates nothing, so isFull() is false (2 != 3), rearAtEnd() is true (2 == 3 - 1), peek() is 2, and peekRear() is 3. Storing 4 at index 0 is circular-queue behavior, and size stays 2 rather than 3.
questions.page: On regular-queue.html: set queue size 3, enqueue 1, 2, 3, dequeue 1, try to enqueue 4, then click isFull?, Peek (Front), and Rear (Tail).
